title: Data Engineering Foundations: Batch and Streaming Pipelines
subtitle: Build reliable data pipelines in Python and DuckDB: file formats, idempotent and incremental loads, partitioned Parquet, quality checks and a first stream.
outcomes: Explain what data engineers build, and choose between batch and streaming, and between ETL and ELT, for a given need
Choose a file format, and explain how Parquet's columns, row groups and statistics make analytical queries cheaper
Write loads that are idempotent and incremental, and partition data so that a single day can be replaced
Build a tested batch pipeline in Python and DuckDB that rejects bad rows with reasons and checks its data before publishing
Process an event stream in micro-batches with a checkpoint, de-duplication and event-time windows
Schedule a pipeline with cron, and explain what an orchestrator adds
prerequisites: Python Programming with PyCharm, or the same Python: functions, files and installing packages with pip. SQL basics (SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and joins), as in SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip. Install Python 3.10 or later and, in a virtual environment, DuckDB, pandas and pytest: python -m pip install duckdb pandas pytest. The labs were tested with DuckDB 1.5, and every dataset comes with them.
description:
Data engineers build the pipelines that carry data from where it's created to where it's used: from apps, sensors and files into tables that analysts, dashboards and machine learning models can trust. This course teaches the foundations by building them. Working with readings from a network of rain gauges, you'll compare ETL with ELT, batch with streaming, and CSV and JSON with Parquet; write loads that can run twice without doubling the data, that pick up only what's new and that replace a single day's partition; and build a small batch pipeline in Python and DuckDB that rejects bad rows with a reason, checks each day before publishing it, and is covered by tests.

The last module looks beyond a single script: scheduling with cron and what an orchestrator adds, a stream processed in micro-batches with a checkpoint, de-duplication and event-time windows, and how to choose tools as data grows. Everything runs on a laptop with no cloud account, and the data is synthetic, made for the course. Afterwards, Orchestrating Data Pipelines with Apache Airflow, Analytics Engineering with dbt and DuckDB, Big Data Processing with Apache Spark, Data Quality, Testing and Data Contracts and Real-Time Data Streaming with Apache Kafka each take one part further.

modules.title: What data engineers build
modules.summary: What a data pipeline is and who depends on it, how batch and streaming differ, and why most teams now load raw data first and transform it where it's stored.

lessons.title: Pipelines and the people who use them
objectives: Describe the stages of a data pipeline, from its sources to the people who use it
Explain what data engineers are responsible for, compared with analysts and data scientists
key_points: A data pipeline moves data from its sources (application databases, files, APIs, sensors, event logs) through ingestion, storage and transformation to where it is used: tables, dashboards, machine learning features or other applications.

Data engineers build and run that path: data arriving on time, complete and correct, kept secure, and processed at a reasonable cost; analysts and data scientists mostly use what the pipelines produce.

Good pipelines keep the raw data as it arrived and build cleaned and modelled layers from it, often called raw, staging and marts (or bronze, silver and gold), so any later layer can be rebuilt when logic changes or a bug is found.
A pipeline is judged by what its users can rely on: freshness (how recent the data is), completeness, correctness, and how quickly problems are noticed and fixed, not only by whether the code ran.
Much of the work is about failure: sources send late, duplicated or malformed data, jobs stop half-way, and a rerun must not corrupt what was already published.

lessons.title: Batch and streaming
objectives: Distinguish batch processing of bounded data from stream processing of unbounded data
Choose between them from the latency a use case really needs
key_points: Batch processing works on a bounded set of data, such as yesterday's files, on a schedule; it is simpler to build, test and rerun, and suits reports, billing and model training.

Stream processing works on unbounded data, events handled continuously as they arrive, with results in seconds; it suits fraud alerts, live monitoring and anything that must react before a batch would run.
Micro-batching sits between the two: a stream is processed in small batches every few seconds or minutes, which is how Spark Structured Streaming works by default.

Event time is when something happened; processing time is when the pipeline sees it. Events arrive late and out of order, so streaming results are grouped by event time, and the pipeline must decide how long to wait for stragglers.

Start from the latency users need: if a result every hour or every day is enough, batch is usually cheaper and easier to run, because streaming adds always-on infrastructure, state to manage and harder reprocessing.

lessons.title: ETL and ELT
objectives: Explain the difference between ETL and ELT, and the trade-offs of each
Explain why keeping the raw data makes a pipeline easier to fix and extend
key_points: ETL (extract, transform, load) transforms data before loading it, so only cleaned results reach the destination; it suited warehouses whose storage and compute were expensive, and is still used when data must be filtered or masked before it lands.

ELT (extract, load, transform) loads the raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse or lakehouse, usually in SQL; cheap storage and scalable query engines made it the common choice, and tools such as dbt are built around it.
Because ELT keeps the raw rows, a new question or a fixed bug needs only the transformation to run again, not a fresh extract from a source that may no longer hold the old data.
Load raw data with every column as text, or with a schema that accepts anything, so a bad value is stored and flagged later instead of making the whole load fail.
Personal and sensitive data needs care in both patterns: with ELT, raw copies sit in the warehouse, so restrict who can read them and drop or mask fields that aren't needed.

"""The same day of rain-gauge readings, processed two ways.

ETL: extract and transform in Python, then load only the result.
ELT: load the raw rows into DuckDB as they are, then transform them there with SQL.
"""

import csv

import duckdb

RAW_FILE = "readings_2024-06-01.csv"
STATIONS_FILE = "stations.csv"


def clean_rain(row, known_stations, seen):
    """Return the row's rain in mm as a float, or None if the row must be rejected.

    Reject a row whose station isn't known, whose rain_mm is missing, not a number or negative,
    or whose (station_id, reading_time) has already been seen.
    """
    # TODO: apply the four rules above; remember each accepted key in seen
    return None


def etl(con):
    with open(STATIONS_FILE, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        known = {row["station_id"] for row in csv.DictReader(f)}
    seen, totals = set(), {}
    with open(RAW_FILE, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            rain = clean_rain(row, known, seen)
            if rain is not None:
                totals[row["station_id"]] = totals.get(row["station_id"], 0.0) + rain
    con.execute("CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE etl_station_daily (station_id VARCHAR, rain_mm DOUBLE)")
    if totals:
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO etl_station_daily VALUES (?, ?)", sorted(totals.items()))


def elt(con):
    # Load: every raw row, every column as text, exactly as it arrived.
    con.execute(f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw_readings AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('{RAW_FILE}', all_varchar = true)")
    con.execute(f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE stations AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('{STATIONS_FILE}', all_varchar = true)")
    # Transform, in SQL, inside the database.
    # TODO: add the same rules as clean_rain() to this query: keep known stations only (join to stations),
    #   keep rows where TRY_CAST(r.rain_mm AS DOUBLE) >= 0, and remove exact duplicate rows (SELECT DISTINCT)
    con.execute("""
        CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE clean_readings AS
        SELECT
            r.station_id,
            CAST(r.reading_time AS TIMESTAMP) AS reading_time,
            TRY_CAST(r.rain_mm AS DOUBLE) AS rain_mm,
            TRY_CAST(r.temp_c AS DOUBLE) AS temp_c
        FROM raw_readings AS r
    """)
    con.execute("""
        CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE elt_station_daily AS
        SELECT station_id, SUM(rain_mm) AS rain_mm FROM clean_readings GROUP BY station_id
    """)


def summary(con, table):
    n, total = con.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*), ROUND(SUM(rain_mm), 1) FROM {table}").fetchone()
    return f"{n} stations, {total} mm"


def main():
    con = duckdb.connect("lab1.duckdb")
    etl(con)
    elt(con)
    print("ETL:", summary(con, "etl_station_daily"))
    print("ELT:", summary(con, "elt_station_daily"))

    raw = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM raw_readings").fetchone()[0]
    clean = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM clean_readings").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"Raw rows kept: {raw}, clean rows: {clean}, rejected: {raw - clean}")

    # A new question, answered from data already in the database: no need to extract again.
    sid, name, ts, rain = con.execute("""
        SELECT c.station_id, s.name, c.reading_time, c.rain_mm
        FROM clean_readings c JOIN stations s USING (station_id)
        ORDER BY c.rain_mm DESC LIMIT 1
    """).fetchone()
    print(f"Wettest reading: {sid} {name} at {ts:%H:%M}, {rain} mm")
    con.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Files and formats
modules.summary: Text formats and columnar Parquet: what each keeps, how readers guess types, and how columns, row groups and statistics make analytical queries cheaper.

lessons.title: CSV and JSON: text that every system reads
objectives: Describe how CSV and JSON Lines store data, and what they leave out
Avoid the type-guessing mistakes that come with text formats
key_points: CSV stores one record per line with fields separated by a delimiter; it has no types and no standard for nulls or dates, and fields that contain the delimiter, quotes or line breaks must be quoted, so every reader has to guess the structure or be told it.

Readers infer types from the values, and their guesses differ: pandas reads a station ID of 001 as the integer 1, losing the leading zeros, unless told dtype={'station_id': 'string'}, while DuckDB's CSV sniffer kept it as text in this course's tests.

JSON represents nested objects and arrays of strings, numbers, booleans and null; JSON Lines, one JSON object per line, can be appended to and split for parallel reading, which is why logs and event streams often use it.
Text formats cost work on every read: values are parsed from strings each time, JSON repeats every key in every record, and a reader must scan whole rows even when it needs one column.

Declare the schema where data enters (types for IDs, dates and amounts, and the encoding, usually UTF-8) instead of trusting inference, and write dates and times in ISO 8601 form, such as 2024-06-01 15:00:00.

lessons.title: Parquet and columnar storage
objectives: Explain how a columnar file is laid out, and why that speeds up analytical queries
Read a Parquet file's schema and statistics
key_points: Parquet is an open, binary, columnar file format: rows are split into row groups, and within each row group every column's values are stored together as a column chunk, compressed and encoded on its own.

The file's footer holds the schema, a physical type such as INT64 and a logical type such as TIMESTAMP for every column, plus statistics for each column chunk, such as its minimum, maximum and null count, so readers needn't guess types.

Column pruning: a query that uses two columns reads only those columns' chunks. Predicate pushdown: a filter such as reading_time >= '2024-06-23' skips row groups whose maximum is earlier, which works best when the data is sorted by that column.
The values in one column are alike, so dictionary and run-length encoding plus a codec such as Snappy or Zstandard (zstd) often make a Parquet file several times smaller than the same data as CSV.

Parquet suits data written once and read many times; its files are immutable, so changing a row means rewriting a file, which is why data is updated by replacing whole files or partitions, or through a table format.

lessons.title: Schemas, compression and table formats
objectives: Choose column types and a compression codec for a dataset
Explain what open table formats add on top of data files
key_points: Choose types for meaning: DATE and TIMESTAMP for times (and say whether a timestamp is UTC or local), DECIMAL rather than floating point for money, and text for identifiers that look like numbers, such as postcodes and IDs with leading zeros.

Snappy compresses and decompresses quickly with a moderate ratio and is a common default; Zstandard usually makes smaller files for a little more CPU; gzip is slower; choose by whether storage or CPU costs more for the workload.

Schemas change: adding a nullable column is usually safe for readers, while renaming or removing a column, or changing its type, breaks them, so changes are agreed with consumers and made backwards compatible where possible.
Avro is a row-oriented binary format with its schema embedded, widely used for event messages; ORC is a columnar format like Parquet, common in the Hadoop and Hive world.

Open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi) keep a transaction log or metadata over a set of data files, usually Parquet, adding atomic commits, schema evolution, time travel to earlier versions and safe concurrent writes.

"""Write readings_june.csv: synthetic hourly readings from eight rain gauges for June 2024 (5,760 rows).

Only random.random() is used, so every Python version writes exactly the same file.
"""

import math
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta

STATIONS = [("001", 277, 0.12), ("002", 306, 0.12), ("003", 336, 0.18), ("004", 298, 0.18),
            ("005", 306, 0.18), ("006", 299, 0.18), ("007", 432, 0.26), ("008", 335, 0.26)]

rng = random.Random(2024)
with open("readings_june.csv", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("station_id,reading_time,rain_mm,temp_c\n")
    for d in range(30):
        day = date(2024, 6, 1) + timedelta(days=d)
        for sid, elev, wet in STATIONS:
            for h in range(24):
                rain = round(-math.log(1 - rng.random()) * 5.0, 1) if rng.random() < wet / 3 else 0.0
                temp = 27.0 + 5.5 * math.sin((h - 9) / 24 * 2 * math.pi) - elev / 300 + (rng.random() - 0.5) * 2
                f.write(f"{sid},{day} {h:02d}:00:00,{rain:.1f},{temp - (2 if rain else 0):.1f}\n")
print("Wrote readings_june.csv")

"""Write the same readings as CSV, JSON Lines and Parquet, then compare what each format keeps."""

import csv
import os

import duckdb
import pandas as pd

os.makedirs("out", exist_ok=True)
con = duckdb.connect()
# Read the source with station_id as text, so the leading zeros (001, 002...) survive.
con.execute("""CREATE TABLE readings AS
               SELECT * FROM read_csv('readings_june.csv', types = {'station_id': 'VARCHAR'})""")

# TODO 1: write the table three times with COPY ... TO:
#   out/readings.csv with a header, out/readings.jsonl with (FORMAT json), and
#   out/readings.parquet with (FORMAT parquet, ROW_GROUP_SIZE 2048), sorted by reading_time

files = {"csv": "out/readings.csv", "jsonl": "out/readings.jsonl", "parquet": "out/readings.parquet"}
counts = {k: con.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM '{p}'").fetchone()[0] for k, p in files.items()}
print("Rows:", counts)

# CSV is only text: the csv module returns strings, and every other reader guesses the types.
with open("out/readings.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print("csv module, first row:", next(csv.DictReader(f)))
guessed = pd.read_csv("out/readings.csv")
print(f"pandas guessed station_id as {guessed['station_id'].dtype}: first value {guessed['station_id'].iloc[0]}")
# TODO 2: read out/readings.csv with pandas again, telling it station_id is a string
#   (dtype={"station_id": "string"}), and print the first value the same way

# Parquet keeps the schema in the file's footer: a physical type and a logical type for every column.
for name, ptype, ctype in con.execute("""
        SELECT name, type, converted_type FROM parquet_schema('out/readings.parquet')
        WHERE name <> 'duckdb_schema'""").fetchall():
    print(f"Parquet column {name:12} stored as {ptype} ({ctype})")

# ...and min/max statistics for every column in every row group.
groups = con.execute("""
    SELECT row_group_id, row_group_num_rows, stats_min_value, stats_max_value
    FROM parquet_metadata('out/readings.parquet')
    WHERE path_in_schema = 'reading_time' ORDER BY row_group_id""").fetchall()
for gid, rows, lo, hi in groups:
    print(f"Row group {gid}: {rows} rows, reading_time {lo} to {hi}")
# TODO 3: a query with WHERE reading_time >= '2024-06-23' can skip every row group whose maximum
#   is earlier than that. Count them into skippable.
skippable = 0
print(f"For reading_time >= '2024-06-23' a reader can skip {skippable} of {len(groups)} row groups")

# Column pruning: a query that needs one column reads only that column's chunks.
chunks = dict(con.execute("""SELECT path_in_schema, SUM(total_compressed_size)
                             FROM parquet_metadata('out/readings.parquet') GROUP BY 1""").fetchall())
print(f"SUM(rain_mm) reads {chunks['rain_mm'] / sum(chunks.values()):.0%} of the column data")

sizes = {k: os.path.getsize(p) for k, p in files.items()}
print("Sizes in bytes:", sizes)
print("Parquet smaller than CSV:", sizes["parquet"] < sizes["csv"])
print("CSV smaller than JSON Lines:", sizes["csv"] < sizes["jsonl"])
for codec in ["uncompressed", "snappy", "zstd"]:
    con.execute(f"COPY readings TO 'out/readings_{codec}.parquet' (FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION {codec})")
    print(f"Parquet with {codec}: {os.path.getsize(f'out/readings_{codec}.parquet')} bytes")

modules.title: Loading data reliably
modules.summary: Loads that can be retried and rerun without corrupting data, that pick up only what's new, and partitions that let one day be replaced on its own.

lessons.title: Idempotent loads
objectives: Explain why pipelines must be safe to rerun, and what makes a load idempotent
Write an idempotent load with delete-and-insert in a transaction, or with an upsert
key_points: An operation is idempotent when running it twice has the same effect as running it once; pipelines need this because retries, reruns after a fix and backfills all run the same load again.
A plain INSERT that appends is not idempotent: running it twice duplicates every row, and the duplicates silently double every total built on them.

Delete-then-insert replaces a whole slice, such as one day: delete the day's rows and insert the new ones inside one transaction, so readers see either the old day or the new one, never a half-loaded mix.

An upsert (or merge) on a key updates the rows that exist and inserts the rest; in DuckDB that's INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE or INSERT OR REPLACE, which need a primary key or unique constraint on the key.
Make each run depend only on its inputs, such as the date it processes, never on the clock: a job that works out 'yesterday' from now() loads a different day when it's rerun tomorrow.

lessons.title: Full and incremental loads
objectives: Compare full reloads with incremental loads
Track a watermark, and handle late-arriving data with a lookback window
key_points: A full load (full refresh) reloads everything on every run; it's simple and corrects any past mistake, but its cost grows with the data, so it suits small tables such as reference lists.

An incremental load fetches only what changed since the last run, using a watermark: the highest value already loaded of a column that only increases, such as an updated_at time, an ID or a file's date, saved in a state table.

Late data defeats a naive watermark: a row stamped 23:59 but committed after the run has moved past it is never loaded, so incremental loads usually re-read a lookback window, such as the last two days, and rely on idempotent writes to absorb the overlap.
Rows deleted in the source are invisible to an updated_at watermark; change data capture (CDC), which reads the source database's change log, captures inserts, updates and deletes in order.
Move the watermark only after the data is safely loaded: if a run stops in between, the next run loads the same files again, which is harmless only because the load is idempotent.

lessons.title: Partitioning
objectives: Explain how partitioning by a column lets readers skip data and writers replace it
Choose a partition column and a granularity
key_points: Partitioning splits a table's files into folders by the value of a column, usually a date, in the Hive style reading_date=2024-06-01/; the value comes from the folder name rather than being stored in every file.
Partition pruning: a query that filters on the partition column reads only the matching folders, so one day of a five-year table means reading one of about 1,800 folders.
Partitions make reruns cheap and safe: a job that rebuilds 2024-06-02 deletes and rewrites only that folder, which is the file version of delete-then-insert for one day.

Partition by a column that most queries filter on and that has a moderate number of values: partitioning by a high-cardinality column such as a customer ID creates many tiny files, and every file adds work to list, open and plan.
Aim for files of tens to hundreds of megabytes; if partitions would be tiny, choose a coarser grain such as month, or don't partition and rely on sorting and Parquet's row group statistics instead.

"""Load daily rain-gauge files into DuckDB: append, idempotent and incremental loads, plus a partitioned copy."""

import glob
import os
import shutil

import duckdb

DB = "warehouse.duckdb"


def setup(con):
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS readings (
        station_id VARCHAR, reading_time TIMESTAMP, rain_mm DOUBLE, temp_c DOUBLE, reading_date DATE)""")
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS load_state (source VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, watermark DATE)")


def select_file(path):
    """A query that reads one landing file with the right types and adds its reading_date."""
    return f"""SELECT station_id, reading_time, rain_mm, temp_c, CAST(reading_time AS DATE) AS reading_date
               FROM read_csv('{path}', types = {{'station_id': 'VARCHAR', 'reading_time': 'TIMESTAMP'}})"""


def day_of(path):
    """landing/readings_2024-06-01.csv -> 2024-06-01"""
    return os.path.basename(path).removeprefix("readings_").removesuffix(".csv")


def load_append(con, path):
    """The naive load: append whatever the file holds."""
    con.execute(f"INSERT INTO readings {select_file(path)}")


def load_day(con, day, path):
    """Idempotent load: replace the day's rows in one transaction, so running it again changes nothing."""
    # TODO: start a transaction with con.begin(); delete the rows whose reading_date is day
    #   (use a ? parameter); insert the file's rows with select_file(path); then con.commit().
    #   If anything fails, call con.rollback() and re-raise the error.
    pass


def load_new_days(con, folder="landing"):
    """Incremental load: only the days after the watermark, then move the watermark forward."""
    row = con.execute("SELECT watermark FROM load_state WHERE source = 'readings'").fetchone()
    watermark = str(row[0]) if row else ""
    # TODO: for each file in sorted(glob.glob(f"{folder}/readings_*.csv")) whose day_of(path) is
    #   later than watermark, call load_day. Then, if any day was loaded, save the newest one with
    #   INSERT OR REPLACE INTO load_state VALUES ('readings', ?). Return the list of days loaded.
    return []


def write_partition(con, day, lake="lake/readings"):
    """Overwrite one date partition of the Parquet copy: remove its folder, then write it again."""
    folder = f"{lake}/reading_date={day}"
    # TODO: remove folder if it exists (shutil.rmtree), create it (os.makedirs), then COPY that day's
    #   rows, without the reading_date column (SELECT * EXCLUDE (reading_date)), to folder/data.parquet


def rows_for(con, day):
    return con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM readings WHERE reading_date = ?", [day]).fetchone()[0]


def main():
    # Start from nothing each time, so this script can be run again and again.
    for path in [DB, DB + ".wal"]:
        if os.path.exists(path):
            os.remove(path)
    shutil.rmtree("lake", ignore_errors=True)
    con = duckdb.connect(DB)
    setup(con)

    print("1. Append the same file twice")
    load_append(con, "landing/readings_2024-06-01.csv")
    load_append(con, "landing/readings_2024-06-01.csv")
    print(f"   rows for 2024-06-01: {rows_for(con, '2024-06-01')} (the file has 64)")
    con.execute("DELETE FROM readings")

    print("2. Idempotent load, run twice")
    load_day(con, "2024-06-01", "landing/readings_2024-06-01.csv")
    load_day(con, "2024-06-01", "landing/readings_2024-06-01.csv")
    print(f"   rows for 2024-06-01: {rows_for(con, '2024-06-01')}")

    print("3. Incremental loads")
    print("   run 1 loaded:", load_new_days(con))
    print("   run 2 loaded:", load_new_days(con) or "nothing new")
    state = con.execute("SELECT watermark FROM load_state").fetchone()
    watermark = state[0] if state else None
    total = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM readings").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"   watermark: {watermark}, rows: {total}")

    print("4. A corrected file for 2024-06-02 arrives")
    rain_008 = "SELECT ROUND(SUM(rain_mm), 1) FROM readings WHERE station_id = '008' AND reading_date = '2024-06-02'"
    before = con.execute(rain_008).fetchone()[0]
    load_day(con, "2024-06-02", "corrections/readings_2024-06-02.csv")
    after = con.execute(rain_008).fetchone()[0]
    print(f"   station 008 on 2024-06-02: {before} mm before, {after} mm after; "
          f"rows for the day: {rows_for(con, '2024-06-02')}")

    print("5. A partitioned Parquet copy")
    for day in ["2024-06-01", "2024-06-02", "2024-06-03"]:
        write_partition(con, day)
    write_partition(con, "2024-06-02")  # a rerun overwrites the partition; it doesn't add to it
    for path in sorted(glob.glob("lake/readings/*/*.parquet")):
        print("  ", path)
    lake = "read_parquet('lake/readings/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)"
    per_day = con.execute(f"SELECT reading_date, COUNT(*) FROM {lake} GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1").fetchall()
    print("   rows per partition:", [(str(d), n) for d, n in per_day])
    con.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: A batch pipeline in Python and DuckDB
modules.summary: Structure a pipeline as small, testable steps, transform in SQL with DuckDB, check each day's data before publishing it, and test the whole thing.

lessons.title: Designing a batch pipeline
objectives: Structure a pipeline as extract, transform, check and load steps that each do one thing
Make a run reproducible from its parameters and visible in its logs
key_points: Split a pipeline into steps with clear inputs and outputs, such as extract, transform, quality checks and load, so each step can be tested, rerun and timed on its own.
Pass the date being processed as a parameter, such as --date 2024-06-01, so any day can be rerun or backfilled and every step works on the same slice of data.
Keep data in layers: raw as it arrived, clean with types and rules applied, rejected rows with the reason each failed, and published tables (marts) that users query.
Log what every run did (rows read, kept and rejected, checks passed), record it in a run table, and exit with a non-zero status on failure so a scheduler or orchestrator can tell it failed.
Keep configuration such as paths and connection details out of the code, in arguments, environment variables or a config file, and never commit passwords or keys.

lessons.title: Transforming data with SQL in DuckDB
objectives: Read files directly with DuckDB and transform them with SQL
Cast values safely and remove duplicates by key
key_points: DuckDB is an in-process analytical database: it runs inside a Python program with no server, keeps a database in one file or in memory, and queries CSV, JSON and Parquet files directly, many at once with a glob such as 'landing/*.csv'.

CAST fails the whole query on one bad value (Conversion Error: Could not convert string 'n/a' to DOUBLE); TRY_CAST returns NULL instead, so bad values can be found and rejected with a reason rather than stopping the run.

Remove duplicates by key with a window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY station_id, reading_time ORDER BY ...) numbers the copies of each key, and keeping number 1, for example with QUALIFY, keeps one row per key.
A LEFT JOIN to a reference table finds rows whose key is unknown, because the reference columns come back NULL; an inner join would drop those rows silently and hide the problem.
Build each layer with CREATE TABLE AS or INSERT ... SELECT, and write Parquet with COPY ... TO; DuckDB uses every CPU core by default and can process data larger than memory by spilling to disk.

Row-level rules send bad rows to a rejected (quarantine) table with a reason, so the good rows still flow and the bad ones can be inspected, fixed at the source and loaded again.

"""A daily batch pipeline for rain-gauge readings.

landing CSV -> raw_readings -> clean_readings (+ rejected_readings) -> quality checks
            -> station_daily (the mart) and lake/readings/reading_date=.../data.parquet

Run one day:    python pipeline.py --date 2024-06-01
Run every day:  python pipeline.py --all
"""

import argparse
import glob
import logging
import os
import shutil
import sys

import duckdb

DB = "rain.duckdb"
READINGS_PER_STATION = 8  # one every three hours
log = logging.getLogger("pipeline")


class QualityError(Exception):
    """Raised when a quality check fails, so nothing is published for that day."""


def connect(path=DB):
    con = duckdb.connect(path)
    con.execute("""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE stations AS
                   SELECT * FROM read_csv('stations.csv', types = {'station_id': 'VARCHAR'})""")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS raw_readings (
        station_id VARCHAR, reading_time VARCHAR, rain_mm VARCHAR, temp_c VARCHAR,
        _row BIGINT, _source_file VARCHAR, _run_date DATE)""")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS clean_readings (
        station_id VARCHAR, reading_time TIMESTAMP, rain_mm DOUBLE, temp_c DOUBLE, reading_date DATE)""")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS rejected_readings (
        station_id VARCHAR, reading_time VARCHAR, rain_mm VARCHAR, temp_c VARCHAR, reason VARCHAR, reading_date DATE)""")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS station_daily (
        reading_date DATE, station_id VARCHAR, name VARCHAR, rain_mm DOUBLE, max_temp_c DOUBLE, readings BIGINT)""")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pipeline_runs (
        run_date DATE, raw_rows BIGINT, clean_rows BIGINT, rejected_rows BIGINT, status VARCHAR)""")
    return con


def replace_day(con, table, date_column, day, select_sql, params=()):
    """Idempotent write: delete the day's rows and insert the new ones in one transaction."""
    con.begin()
    try:
        con.execute(f"DELETE FROM {table} WHERE {date_column} = ?", [day])
        con.execute(f"INSERT INTO {table} {select_sql}", list(params))
        con.commit()
    except Exception:
        con.rollback()
        raise


def extract(con, day):
    """Copy the day's landing file into raw_readings as text, exactly as it arrived."""
    path = f"landing/readings_{day}.csv"
    replace_day(con, "raw_readings", "_run_date", day, f"""
        SELECT station_id, reading_time, rain_mm, temp_c, ROW_NUMBER() OVER () AS _row,
               '{path}' AS _source_file, DATE '{day}' AS _run_date
        FROM read_csv('{path}', all_varchar = true)""")
    return con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM raw_readings WHERE _run_date = ?", [day]).fetchone()[0]


def transform(con, day):
    """Type the raw rows, give every bad row a reason, and split them into clean and rejected."""
    con.execute("""
        CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE checked AS
        WITH typed AS (
            SELECT r.*,
                   TRY_CAST(r.reading_time AS TIMESTAMP) AS ts,
                   TRY_CAST(r.rain_mm AS DOUBLE) AS rain,
                   TRY_CAST(r.temp_c AS DOUBLE) AS temp,
                   s.station_id IS NOT NULL AS known_station,
                   ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY r.station_id, r.reading_time ORDER BY r._row) AS copy_number
            FROM raw_readings AS r
            LEFT JOIN stations AS s ON r.station_id = s.station_id
            WHERE r._run_date = ?
        )
        SELECT *,
            NULL AS reason  -- TODO: a CASE expression giving each bad row its reason (see below)
        FROM typed
    """, [day])
    # TODO (above): replace NULL AS reason with a CASE expression that gives, in this order:
    #   'unknown station' when not known_station, 'bad timestamp' when ts is null,
    #   'missing rain' when rain is null, 'negative rain' when rain < 0,
    #   'duplicate' when copy_number > 1, and NULL (no reason) for a good row.
    replace_day(con, "clean_readings", "reading_date", day, """
        SELECT station_id, ts, rain, temp, CAST(ts AS DATE) FROM checked WHERE reason IS NULL""")
    replace_day(con, "rejected_readings", "reading_date", day, """
        SELECT station_id, reading_time, rain_mm, temp_c, reason, ? FROM checked WHERE reason IS NOT NULL""",
                [day])


def quality_checks(con, day):
    """Return a list of (check name, passed) for the day's clean rows."""
    one = lambda sql: con.execute(sql, [day]).fetchone()[0]  # noqa: E731
    checks = [
        ("rows_present", one("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM clean_readings WHERE reading_date = ?") > 0),
        ("no_null_keys", one("""SELECT COUNT(*) FROM clean_readings WHERE reading_date = ?
                                AND (station_id IS NULL OR reading_time IS NULL)""") == 0),
        ("rain_in_range", one("""SELECT COUNT(*) FROM clean_readings WHERE reading_date = ?
                                 AND NOT rain_mm BETWEEN 0 AND 200""") == 0),
    ]
    # TODO: add two more checks to the list:
    #   unique_station_time: no (station_id, reading_time) appears twice in the day's clean rows
    #   all_stations_reported: every station in stations has READINGS_PER_STATION clean rows that day
    return checks


def load(con, day):
    """Publish the day: rebuild its rows in the mart and overwrite its partition in the lake."""
    replace_day(con, "station_daily", "reading_date", day, """
        SELECT c.reading_date, c.station_id, s.name, ROUND(SUM(c.rain_mm), 1), MAX(c.temp_c), COUNT(*)
        FROM clean_readings AS c JOIN stations AS s ON c.station_id = s.station_id
        WHERE c.reading_date = ? GROUP BY ALL""", [day])
    folder = f"lake/readings/reading_date={day}"
    shutil.rmtree(folder, ignore_errors=True)
    os.makedirs(folder)
    con.execute(f"""COPY (SELECT * EXCLUDE (reading_date) FROM clean_readings WHERE reading_date = '{day}')
                    TO '{folder}/data.parquet' (FORMAT parquet)""")


def run(con, day):
    raw = extract(con, day)
    transform(con, day)
    clean = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM clean_readings WHERE reading_date = ?", [day]).fetchone()[0]
    checks = quality_checks(con, day)
    failed = [name for name, ok in checks if not ok]
    status = "failed: " + ", ".join(failed) if failed else "published"
    replace_day(con, "pipeline_runs", "run_date", day, "SELECT ?, ?, ?, ?, ?", [day, raw, clean, raw - clean, status])
    log.info("%s: raw %d, clean %d, rejected %d, checks %d/%d passed",
             day, raw, clean, raw - clean, len(checks) - len(failed), len(checks))
    if failed:
        raise QualityError(f"{day}: {', '.join(failed)}")
    load(con, day)


def main(argv=None):
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    group = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)
    group.add_argument("--date", help="the day to process, as YYYY-MM-DD")
    group.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="process every file in landing/")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    days = [args.date] if args.date else sorted(
        os.path.basename(p)[9:19] for p in glob.glob("landing/readings_*.csv"))
    con = connect()
    try:
        for day in days:
            run(con, day)
    except QualityError as e:
        log.error("quality checks failed, nothing published for %s", e)
        return 1
    finally:
        con.close()
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

print("station_daily rows:", con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM station_daily").fetchone()[0])

modules.summary: Run pipelines on a schedule and see what an orchestrator adds, process an event stream in micro-batches, and choose tools as data grows.

lessons.title: Scheduling and orchestration
objectives: Schedule a pipeline with cron, and explain its limits
Explain what an orchestrator adds: dependencies, retries, backfills and monitoring
key_points: cron runs commands on a schedule of five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week): 15 6 * * * runs at 06:15 every day. It comes with Linux and macOS and is fine for a single job on one machine.
cron knows nothing about dependencies between jobs, doesn't retry, keeps no history of runs and can't easily rerun a range of past dates, so failures have to be noticed some other way.

An orchestrator runs a workflow as a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of tasks: each task starts when the tasks it depends on have succeeded, and tasks that don't depend on each other can run in parallel.
Orchestrators add retries with delays, alerts, a history and logs for every run, and backfills (runs for past dates), which work only if each task processes the date it is given and is idempotent.

Widely used open-source orchestrators include Apache Airflow, Dagster and Prefect; they schedule and watch the work, while the heavy processing happens in the tools they call, such as DuckDB, Spark or a warehouse.

lessons.title: Streams: events, offsets and windows
objectives: Explain how an event log, offsets and consumer checkpoints work
Group events into event-time windows, and handle duplicates and late events
key_points: An event stream is an append-only log of records, such as a Kafka topic; consumers read it in order and track their position as an offset, so after a restart they carry on from the last committed offset instead of starting again.
Delivery is usually at-least-once: after a failure some events are delivered again, so consumers de-duplicate by an event ID or make their writes idempotent.
Committing results and the new offset in one transaction gives exactly-once results for that sink: both are saved or neither is, so a crash between them can't double-count or skip events.
A tumbling window groups events into fixed, non-overlapping intervals of event time, such as 08:00-08:10; sliding (or hopping) windows overlap, and a session window closes after a gap in activity.

A watermark is the pipeline's estimate of how far event time has got, such as the latest event time seen minus five minutes; a window is closed and published once the watermark passes its end, and events arriving after that are late.
Handle late events on purpose: drop them, set them aside, or update the published result; allowing more lateness gives more complete results but publishes them later.

lessons.title: Choosing tools as data grows
objectives: Recognise when one machine is enough and when distributed processing is needed
Describe what warehouses, lakehouses and transformation tools each add
key_points: One machine goes a long way: DuckDB or pandas on a laptop or a single server handles many gigabytes and is simpler and cheaper to run than a cluster; move on when jobs no longer fit the time or memory available.
Distributed engines such as Apache Spark split data into partitions processed in parallel on many machines; they handle far more data, but bring cluster costs, network shuffles and harder debugging.

Cloud data warehouses such as BigQuery, Snowflake and Amazon Redshift run SQL over large tables as managed services; a lakehouse keeps open files such as Parquet in object storage, under a table format, and lets several engines query them.

dbt organises SQL transformations in the warehouse as tested, documented models that run in dependency order; ingestion tools copy data from common sources into the warehouse, so less extraction code is written by hand.

Choose tools by the data's size, the freshness users need, the team's skills and the budget, and keep this course's foundations whatever the tools: raw data kept, idempotent and incremental loads, partitions, quality checks and clear ownership.

"""Write events.jsonl: one hour of tipping-bucket events from three rain gauges, in the order they arrive.

Each event is one tip of a gauge's bucket (0.2 mm of rain). Most arrive within 90 seconds of happening,
a few arrive more than ten minutes late, and some are delivered twice. Only random.random() is used,
so every Python version writes exactly the same file.
"""

import json
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import random

rng = random.Random(7)
start = datetime(2024, 6, 1, 8, 0, 0)
events = []
for station, tips in [("001", 70), ("005", 110), ("007", 90)]:
    times = sorted(int(rng.random() * 3600) for _ in range(tips))
    for seq, t in enumerate(times, 1):
        happened = start + timedelta(seconds=t)
        delay = 600 + int(rng.random() * 300) if rng.random() < 0.03 else int(rng.random() * 90)
        event = {"event_id": f"{station}-{seq:04d}", "station_id": station,
                 "event_time": happened.isoformat(), "rain_mm": 0.2}
        events.append((happened + timedelta(seconds=delay), event))
        if rng.random() < 0.04:  # delivered again a little later
            events.append((happened + timedelta(seconds=delay + 30 + int(rng.random() * 90)), event))
events.sort(key=lambda pair: (pair[0], pair[1]["event_id"]))
with open("events.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for _arrived, event in events:
        f.write(json.dumps(event) + "\n")
print(f"Wrote {len(events)} events to events.jsonl")

"""Consume rain-gauge events in micro-batches: a checkpoint, de-duplication and 10-minute event-time windows.

python consumer.py                   process every new event, then stop
python consumer.py --max-batches 2   stop after two batches, as if the consumer had crashed
python consumer.py --reset           forget the checkpoint and all state, and start again
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

import duckdb

EVENTS = "events.jsonl"
STATE = "stream_state.duckdb"
BATCH_SIZE = 50
WINDOW = timedelta(minutes=10)
ALLOWED_LATENESS = timedelta(minutes=5)


def window_start(ts):
    """The start of the 10-minute tumbling window that ts falls in: 08:47:12 -> 08:40:00."""
    # TODO: return ts with its minutes rounded down to a multiple of 10, and seconds and microseconds set to 0
    return ts


def setup(con):
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS checkpoint (next_offset BIGINT, max_event_time TIMESTAMP)")
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS seen (event_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY)")
    con.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accepted (
        event_id VARCHAR, station_id VARCHAR, event_time TIMESTAMP, rain_mm DOUBLE, window_start TIMESTAMP)""")
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS late_events (event_id VARCHAR, station_id VARCHAR, event_time TIMESTAMP)")
    if con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM checkpoint").fetchone()[0] == 0:
        con.execute("INSERT INTO checkpoint VALUES (0, NULL)")


def process_batch(con, lines, offset, watermark):
    """Process one batch in a single transaction: the results and the new checkpoint commit together."""
    counts = {"new": 0, "duplicates": 0, "late": 0}
    max_time = con.execute("SELECT max_event_time FROM checkpoint").fetchone()[0]
    con.begin()
    for line in lines:
        e = json.loads(line)
        ts = datetime.fromisoformat(e["event_time"])
        # TODO: if e["event_id"] is already in the seen table, count it as a duplicate and skip it
        #   (continue); otherwise insert it into seen
        start = window_start(ts)
        if watermark is not None and start + WINDOW <= watermark:
            # Its window has already closed: set it aside instead of changing a published result.
            con.execute("INSERT INTO late_events VALUES (?, ?, ?)", [e["event_id"], e["station_id"], ts])
            counts["late"] += 1
            continue
        con.execute("INSERT INTO accepted VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                    [e["event_id"], e["station_id"], ts, e["rain_mm"], start])
        counts["new"] += 1
        max_time = ts if max_time is None else max(max_time, ts)
    con.execute("DELETE FROM checkpoint")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO checkpoint VALUES (?, ?)", [offset + len(lines), max_time])
    con.commit()
    return counts


def report(con, watermark):
    print("Windows (event time):")
    for start, station, tips, rain in con.execute("""
            SELECT window_start, station_id, COUNT(*), ROUND(SUM(rain_mm), 1)
            FROM accepted GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY window_start, station_id""").fetchall():
        state = "closed" if watermark is not None and start + WINDOW <= watermark else "open"
        print(f"  {start:%H:%M}-{start + WINDOW:%H:%M} station {station}: {tips} tips, {rain} mm ({state})")
    accepted, late = (con.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {t}").fetchone()[0] for t in ["accepted", "late_events"])
    print(f"Accepted {accepted} events; {late} late events set aside")


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--max-batches", type=int, default=None)
    parser.add_argument("--reset", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.reset:
        for path in [STATE, STATE + ".wal"]:
            if os.path.exists(path):
                os.remove(path)
    con = duckdb.connect(STATE)
    setup(con)
    offset = con.execute("SELECT next_offset FROM checkpoint").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"Starting at offset {offset}")
    with open(EVENTS, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
    batches = 0
    duplicates = 0
    while offset < len(lines) and (args.max_batches is None or batches < args.max_batches):
        max_time = con.execute("SELECT max_event_time FROM checkpoint").fetchone()[0]
        watermark = max_time - ALLOWED_LATENESS if max_time else None
        batch = lines[offset:offset + BATCH_SIZE]
        counts = process_batch(con, batch, offset, watermark)
        duplicates += counts["duplicates"]
        print(f"Batch at offsets {offset}-{offset + len(batch) - 1}: {counts['new']} new, "
              f"{counts['duplicates']} duplicates, {counts['late']} late")
        offset += len(batch)
        batches += 1
    max_time = con.execute("SELECT max_event_time FROM checkpoint").fetchone()[0]
    watermark = max_time - ALLOWED_LATENESS if max_time else None
    print(f"Stopped at offset {offset} of {len(lines)}; watermark {watermark}")
    report(con, watermark)
    con.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: ts.minute % 10 is how far into its window an event is: 47 % 10 is 7, so 08:47 belongs to the 08:40 window.
con.execute("SELECT 1 FROM seen WHERE event_id = ?", [event_id]).fetchone() returns None for a new ID.
Each batch's watermark comes from the batches before it, and the checkpoint is committed with the batch's results, so a restarted consumer sees exactly the same batches as before.

project.title: Build a week-long rain-gauge pipeline
project.brief: A network of eight rain gauges sends one CSV file a day, and a team planning reservoir releases needs daily figures per station and per climate zone that it can trust. Generate a week of data with make_capstone_data.py, then build a batch pipeline in Python and DuckDB (your module 4 lab is a good start) that loads every file, keeps the raw rows, rejects bad rows with a reason, checks each day before publishing it, and publishes a station_daily mart, a zone_daily mart and a partitioned Parquet lake. The data has the problems real feeds have: duplicates; missing, negative and malformed values; a station that isn't on the list; a day when one station stops reporting; a file whose columns arrive in a different order; and a correction for 2024-06-02 that arrives a week later. Loads must be idempotent and incremental (driven by a watermark), every run must be logged, and a short design note explains your choices, including whether any part needs streaming.

The output of a run over the whole week, of a second run that finds nothing new, and of loading the correction for 2024-06-02
Query results: the run log, the rejected rows counted by reason, and zone_daily for the week
A README that explains how to install and run the pipeline, with a crontab line (or orchestrator schedule) to run it daily
A design note of about a page: ETL or ELT, how reruns, the late correction and the incomplete day are handled, whether any part needs streaming, and what would change with 100 times the data

"""Write the capstone's data: a week of rain-gauge files with the problems real feeds have.

Creates stations.csv, landing/readings_2024-06-01.csv ... readings_2024-06-07.csv and, a week later,
corrections/readings_2024-06-02.csv. The readings are synthetic. Only random.random() is used, so every
Python version writes exactly the same files.
"""

import math
import os
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta

STATIONS = [("001", "Dori", "Sahelian", 0.12), ("002", "Djibo", "Sahelian", 0.12),
            ("003", "Ouahigouya", "Sudano-Sahelian", 0.18), ("004", "Kaya", "Sudano-Sahelian", 0.18),
            ("005", "Ouagadougou", "Sudano-Sahelian", 0.18), ("006", "Koudougou", "Sudano-Sahelian", 0.18),
            ("007", "Bobo-Dioulasso", "Sudanian", 0.26), ("008", "Gaoua", "Sudanian", 0.26)]
rng = random.Random(2406)


def pick(items):
    return items[int(rng.random() * len(items))]


def day_rows(day):
    rows = []
    for sid, _name, _zone, wet in STATIONS:
        for h in range(0, 24, 3):
            rain = round(-math.log(1 - rng.random()) * 5.0, 1) if rng.random() < wet else 0.0
            temp = 26.0 + 5.5 * math.sin((h - 9) / 24 * 2 * math.pi) + (rng.random() - 0.5) * 2 - (2 if rain else 0)
            rows.append([sid, f"{day} {h:02d}:00:00", f"{rain:.1f}", f"{temp:.1f}"])
    return rows


def add_problems(rows, day):
    bad = [pick(rows)[:],  # an exact duplicate
           [pick(STATIONS)[0], f"{day} 10:30:00", "", "30.5"],  # missing rain
           [pick(STATIONS)[0], f"{day} 11:30:00", "-0.4", "31.0"],  # negative rain
           ["0" + str(10 + int(rng.random() * 80)), f"{day} 12:00:00", "0.0", "32.0"],  # unknown station
           [pick(STATIONS)[0], f"{day}T25:00", "0.0", "29.0"]]  # malformed timestamp
    for row in bad[: 2 + int(rng.random() * 4)]:
        rows.insert(int(rng.random() * len(rows)), row)
    return rows


def write(path, rows, header=("station_id", "reading_time", "rain_mm", "temp_c")):
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path) or ".", exist_ok=True)
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(",".join(header) + "\n")
        for r in rows:
            f.write(",".join(r) + "\n")


with open("stations.csv", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("station_id,name,climate_zone\n" + "".join(f"{s},{n},{z}\n" for s, n, z, _w in STATIONS))
for d in range(7):
    day = str(date(2024, 6, 1) + timedelta(days=d))
    clean = day_rows(day)
    rows = add_problems([r[:] for r in clean], day)
    if day == "2024-06-04":  # station 003's modem failed in the afternoon: three readings never arrive
        rows = [r for r in rows if not (r[0] == "003" and r[1] >= f"{day} 15:00:00")]
    if day == "2024-06-05":  # a firmware update swapped the column order
        write(f"landing/readings_{day}.csv", [[r[0], r[1], r[3], r[2]] for r in rows],
              header=("station_id", "reading_time", "temp_c", "rain_mm"))
        continue
    write(f"landing/readings_{day}.csv", rows)
    if day == "2024-06-02":  # a week later: station 006's readings were re-checked and corrected
        fixed = [[r[0], r[1], f"{float(r[2]) * 1.5:.1f}" if r[0] == "006" else r[2], r[3]] for r in clean]
        write(f"corrections/readings_{day}.csv", fixed)
print("Wrote stations.csv, 7 files in landing/ and 1 in corrections/")
